title: OS-Liberty-Puppet
short_description: This complexe appliance deploys a Controller node and a custom number of computes node
long_description:
[Documentation](https://chameleoncloud.org/appliances/44/docs/)
This complexe appliance deploys a Controller node and a custom number of computes node. It relies on Puppet Openstack modules (ex : https://git.openstack.org/cgit/openstack/puppet-keystone/ ) to deploy Openstack Liberty.

The dashboard is available on the controller on port 8080. Username admin, the password is asked when you run the stack, it's default value is demo

The main steps of the deployment are :
- Populate /etc/hosts so that each node can join the others using their hostnames.
- Bootstrap puppet server : It install a puppet server on the controller
- OS modules : It install the OS modules in the correct folder for Puppet to recognize them, it also update the hiera data to set which modules to apply on which
nodes ( module controller on the controller node, compute module on the other.)
- Run puppet agent on the controller node and make some basic network configuration ( create public and private network ), add Cirros image to glance.
- Run puppet agent on compute nodes

This complexe appliance relies on 2 images :
- OS-Liberty-Puppet_base : It's a CC-Ubuntu14.04 image with Heat agent and Puppet agent installed on it.
- OS-Liberty-Puppet_controller : It's a OS-Liberty-Puppet_base image with preinstalled Openstack packages to speed up the Openstack deployment. The list of preinstall packages is here
The script to generate these 2 images is available here (branch controller for the controller image )

The whole deployment takes approximately 20 - 25 min. ( Depending on the number of compute nodes and if you're running it on UC or TACC )

Liberty OpenStack

environment_setup.arguments:
# This describes what is deployed by this template.
description: "Deploys Openstack Liberty without network isolation : The public network of the OS instance is the sharednet of Chameleon. We end up with a Controller (storage, network, horizon, ...) and a configurable number of Compute nodes."

# This defines the minimum Heat version required by this template.
heat_template_version: 2015-10-15

# The resources section defines what OpenStack resources are to be deployed and
# how they should be configured.
resources:

  ##########
  # Setting up resources (Instance and IP)
  ##########
  controller_floating_ip:
    type: OS::Nova::FloatingIP
    properties:
      pool: ext-net

  router_port:
    type: OS::Neutron::Port
    properties:
      name: router-port
      network: sharednet1

  controller:
    type: OS::Nova::Server
    properties:
      name:
        str_replace:
          template: $stack_name_controller
          params:
            $stack_name: { get_param: "OS::stack_name" }
      flavor: baremetal
      image: OS-Liberty-Puppet_controller
      key_name: { get_param: key_name }
      networks:
         - network: sharednet1
      scheduler_hints: { reservation: { get_param: reservation_id } }
      user_data_format: SOFTWARE_CONFIG
      software_config_transport: POLL_SERVER_HEAT

  compute_nodes:
    type: OS::Heat::ResourceGroup
    properties:
      count: { get_param: compute_node_count }
      resource_def:
        type: OS::Nova::Server
        properties:
          name:
            str_replace:
              template: $stack_name_compute-%index%
              params:
                $stack_name: { get_param: "OS::stack_name" }
          flavor: baremetal
          image: OS-Liberty-Puppet_base
          key_name: { get_param: key_name }
          networks:
             - network: sharednet1
          scheduler_hints: { reservation: { get_param: reservation_id } }
          user_data_format: SOFTWARE_CONFIG
          software_config_transport: POLL_SERVER_HEAT

  controller_ip_association:
    type: OS::Nova::FloatingIPAssociation
    properties:
      floating_ip: { get_resource: controller_floating_ip }
      server_id: { get_resource: controller }

  ##########
  # Configure hostname and /etc/hosts
  # TODO : Find a simpler way to do this
  ##########
  export_hosts:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareConfig
    properties:
      outputs:
        - name: hosts
      group: script
      config: |
        #!/bin/sh
        export PATH=$PATH:/opt/puppetlabs/bin
        (echo -n $(facter ipaddress); echo -n ' '; echo -n $(facter hostname); echo -n ' '; echo $(facter hostname).openstacklocal) > ${heat_outputs_path}.hosts

  populate_hosts:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareConfig
    properties:
      inputs:
        - name: hosts_srv
        - name: hosts_compute
      group: script
      config: |
        #!/usr/bin/env python
        import ast
        import os
        import string
        import subprocess
        hosts_srv = os.getenv('hosts_srv')
        hosts_compute = os.getenv('hosts_compute')
        if hosts_compute is not None:
            hosts_compute = ast.literal_eval(string.replace(hosts_compute, '\n', '\\n'))
        with open('/etc/hosts', 'a') as hosts_file:
          hosts_file.write(hosts_srv.rstrip() + '\n')
          for ip_host in hosts_compute.values():
              hosts_file.write(ip_host.rstrip() + '\n')

  export_hosts_srv:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareDeployment
    properties:
      config: { get_resource: export_hosts }
      server: { get_resource: controller }
      signal_transport: HEAT_SIGNAL

  export_hosts_compute:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareDeploymentGroup
    properties:
      config: { get_resource: export_hosts }
      servers: { get_attr: [compute_nodes, refs_map]}
      signal_transport: HEAT_SIGNAL

  populate_hosts_srv:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareDeployment
    depends_on:
      - export_hosts_srv
      - export_hosts_compute
    properties:
      config: { get_resource: populate_hosts }
      server: { get_resource: controller }
      signal_transport: HEAT_SIGNAL
      input_values:
        hosts_srv: { get_attr: [ export_hosts_srv, hosts ] }
        hosts_compute: { get_attr: [ export_hosts_compute, hosts ] }

  populate_hosts_compute:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareDeploymentGroup
    depends_on:
      - export_hosts_srv
      - export_hosts_compute
    properties:
      config: { get_resource: populate_hosts }
      servers: { get_attr: [compute_nodes, refs_map]}
      signal_transport: HEAT_SIGNAL
      input_values:
        hosts_srv: { get_attr: [ export_hosts_srv, hosts ] }
        hosts_compute: { get_attr: [ export_hosts_compute, hosts ] }

  ##########
  # Bootstrap Puppet Server
  ##########
  puppet_bootstrap_cfg:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareConfig
    properties:
      group: script
      config:
        str_replace:
          template: |
            #!/bin/sh
            cd /tmp
            #Fix host name ( Upperase to lowercase and '_' to '-' )
            export controller_name=$(echo $controller_heat_name | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr '_' '-')
            export stack_name=$(echo $stack_heat_name | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr '_' '-')
            # Remove puppet key (will be regenerate)
            rm -f /etc/puppetlabs/puppet/ssl/private_keys/${controller_name}.openstacklocal.pem
            #Clone g5k repo then copy hiera and modules
            git clone -b CC_liberty https://github.com/dloup/xp5k-openstack.git
            export MODULE_DIR=xp5k-openstack/provision/puppet/modules
            export HIERA_TEMPLATES_DIR=xp5k-openstack/scenarios/liberty_CC/hiera/templates
            export PUPPET_DIR=/etc/puppetlabs/code/environments
            mkdir $PUPPET_DIR/bootstrap
            cp -r $MODULE_DIR $PUPPET_DIR/bootstrap/
            cp -r $HIERA_TEMPLATES_DIR $PUPPET_DIR/bootstrap/hieradata
            #Generate Hiera data for puppet-server and controller
            mv $PUPPET_DIR/bootstrap/hieradata/nodes/puppetserver_controller.yaml $PUPPET_DIR/bootstrap/hieradata/nodes/${controller_name}.openstacklocal.yaml
            sed -i "s/host1/${controller_name}.openstacklocal/g" $PUPPET_DIR/bootstrap/hieradata/nodes/${controller_name}.openstacklocal.yaml
            #Generate hiera data for compute nodes
            current_instance=0
            nb_compute=$compute_node_count
            while [ $current_instance -lt $nb_compute ]
            do
              echo "- ${stack_name}-compute-${current_instance}.openstacklocal" >> $PUPPET_DIR/bootstrap/hieradata/nodes/${controller_name}.openstacklocal.yaml
              cp $PUPPET_DIR/bootstrap/hieradata/nodes/compute.yaml $PUPPET_DIR/bootstrap/hieradata/nodes/${stack_name}-compute-${current_instance}.openstacklocal.yaml
              current_instance=$(($current_instance+1))
            done
            #Bootstrap Puppet Server
            eatmydata /opt/puppetlabs/bin/puppet apply --environment bootstrap -e 'include xp,xp::locales,xp::puppet::server'
            sync
            #Free port 8080 : Puppetdb listen for clear HTTP on 8082 instead of 8080
            sed -i "s/port = 8080/port = 8082/g" /etc/puppetlabs/puppetdb/conf.d/jetty.ini
            service puppetdb restart

          params:
            $controller_heat_name: { get_attr: [controller, name] }
            $stack_heat_name: { get_param: "OS::stack_name" }
            $controller_public_address: { get_attr: [controller, first_address] }
            $compute_node_count: { get_param: compute_node_count }

  puppet_bootstrap_deploy:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareDeployment
    depends_on:
      - populate_hosts_srv
      - populate_hosts_compute
    properties:
      config: { get_resource: puppet_bootstrap_cfg }
      server: { get_resource: controller }
      signal_transport: HEAT_SIGNAL

  ##########
  # Copy Openstack Puppet modules in Puppet directory
  ##########
  os_modules_cfg:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareConfig
    properties:
      group: script
      config:
        str_replace:
          template: |
            #!/bin/sh
            cd /tmp
            #Fix host name ( remove upperase to lower case and '_' to '-' )
            export controller_name=$(echo $controller_heat_name | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr '_' '-')
            export MODULE_DIR=xp5k-openstack/provision/puppet/modules
            export HIERA_TEMPLATES_DIR=xp5k-openstack/scenarios/liberty_CC/hiera/templates
            export PUPPET_DIR=/etc/puppetlabs/code/environments
            export SCENARIO_CC=xp5k-openstack/scenarios/liberty_CC
            #Copy modules to prod env
            cp -r $MODULE_DIR $PUPPET_DIR/production/
            tar xzf $SCENARIO_CC/puppet/modules-openstack.tar.gz -C $PUPPET_DIR/production/
            cp -r $SCENARIO_CC/puppet/modules/scenario $PUPPET_DIR/production/modules-scenario
            #Copy and update hiera data
            cp -r $PUPPET_DIR/bootstrap/hieradata/* $PUPPET_DIR/production/hieradata
            sed -i "s/#Uncomment after OS modules copy//g" $PUPPET_DIR/production/hieradata/nodes/${controller_name}.openstacklocal.yaml
            echo "
            scenario::openstack::admin_password: $OS_password
            scenario::openstack::controller_public_address: $controller_public_address
            scenario::openstack::storage_public_address: $controller_public_address" >> $PUPPET_DIR/production/hieradata/common.yaml
            #Patch OS
            sed -i '24s/apache2/httpd/' $PUPPET_DIR/production/modules-openstack/horizon/manifests/params.pp
            sed -i 's/F78372A06FF50C80464FC1B4F7B8CEA6056E8E56/0A9AF2115F4687BD29803A206B73A36E6026DFCA/' $PUPPET_DIR/production/modules-openstack/rabbitmq/manifests/repo/apt.pp
          params:
            $controller_heat_name: { get_attr: [controller, name] }
            $controller_public_address: { get_attr: [controller, first_address] }
            $OS_password: { get_param: OS_password }

  os_modules_deploy:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareDeployment
    depends_on: puppet_bootstrap_deploy
    properties:
      config: { get_resource: os_modules_cfg }
      server: { get_resource: controller }
      signal_transport: HEAT_SIGNAL


  ##########
  # Run Puppet agent on Controller and add basic configuration for Openstack
  ##########
  puppet_controller_cfg:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareConfig
    properties:
      group: script
      config:
        str_replace:
          template: |
            #!/bin/bash
            #Fix host name ( Upperase to lower case and '_' to '-' )
            export controller_name=$(echo $controller_heat_name | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr '_' '-')
            /opt/puppetlabs/bin/puppet agent -t --server ${controller_name}.openstacklocal > /root/puppet.log 2>&1 || true
            #Basic OS configuration
            source /root/adminrc
              ## Rules (allow SSH and ICMP)
            nova secgroup-add-rule default tcp 22 22 0.0.0.0/0
            nova secgroup-add-rule default icmp -1 -1 0.0.0.0/0
              ## Public Bridge
            ovs-vsctl add-port br-ex eth0 && ip addr flush eth0 && dhclient -nw br-ex
              ## Create xs flavor
            nova flavor-create m1.xs auto 2048 4 2 --is-public True
              ## Images (Cirros and Debian)
            /usr/bin/wget -q -O /tmp/cirros.img http://download.cirros-cloud.net/0.3.4/cirros-0.3.4-x86_64-disk.img
            glance image-create --name="Cirros" --visibility public --disk-format=qcow2 --container-format=bare --property architecture=x86_64 --progress --file /tmp/cirros.img
              ## Network
            neutron net-create public --provider:physical_network external --provider:network_type flat --router:external True
            neutron net-create private
            export host_ip=`/opt/puppetlabs/bin/facter ipaddress`
              ## TACC
            if [[ $host_ip =~ 10\.40\.[0-1]\.[0-9]{1,3} ]]; then
              neutron subnet-create public 10.40.0.0/23 --name public-subnet --gateway 10.40.1.254 --disable-dhcp --allocation-pool start=$router_ip,end=$router_ip
              ## UC
            elif [[ $host_ip =~ 10\.140\.8[0-3]\.[0-9]{1,3} ]]; then
              neutron subnet-create public 10.140.80.0/22 --name public-subnet --gateway 10.140.83.254 --disable-dhcp --allocation-pool start=$router_ip,end=$router_ip
            else
              echo "Can't create network configuration because the controller host is not on the TACC sharednet neither on the UC sharednet"
              exit 1
            fi
            neutron subnet-create private 192.168.0.0/24 --name private-subnet --dns-nameserver 8.8.8.8 --allocation-pool start=192.168.0.10,end=192.168.0.200
            neutron router-create main_router
            neutron router-gateway-set main_router public --fixed-ip subnet_id=public-subnet,ip_address=$router_ip
            neutron router-interface-add main_router private-subnet
          params:
            $controller_heat_name: { get_attr: [controller, name] }
            $router_ip: { get_attr: [router_port, fixed_ips, 0, ip_address] }

  puppet_compute_cfg:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareConfig
    properties:
      group: script
      config:
        str_replace:
          template: |
            #!/bin/bash
            #Fix host name ( Upperase to lower case and '_' to '-' )
            export controller_name=$(echo $controller_heat_name | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | tr '_' '-')
            /opt/puppetlabs/bin/puppet agent -t --server ${controller_name}.openstacklocal > /root/puppet.log 2>&1 || true
          params:
            $controller_heat_name: { get_attr: [controller, name] }

  puppet_controller_deploy:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareDeployment
    depends_on: os_modules_deploy
    properties:
      config: { get_resource: puppet_controller_cfg }
      server: { get_resource: controller }
      signal_transport: HEAT_SIGNAL

  puppet_compute_deploy:
    type: OS::Heat::SoftwareDeploymentGroup
    depends_on: puppet_controller_deploy
    properties:
      config: { get_resource: puppet_compute_cfg }
      servers: { get_attr: [compute_nodes, refs_map]}
      signal_transport: HEAT_SIGNAL

# The parameters section gathers configuration from the user.
parameters:
  key_name:
    type: string
    description: 'Name of a KeyPair to enable SSH access to the instance'
    default: default
    constraints:
    - custom_constraint: nova.keypair

title: MPI+Spack Bare Metal Cluster
short_description: This template sets up an HPC cluster with master and worker nodes, with MPI (MPICH and OpenMPI) and Spack available.
long_description:
This template sets up an HPC cluster with master and worker nodes, with MPI (MPICH and OpenMPI) and Spack available. A temporary bootstrap node handles the setup and configuration, and the users can load MPI or install/load other packages using Spack or Lmod(Lua Modules).

This appliance accepts the following parameters:

reservation_id: ID of the Blazar reservation for master and worker nodes.
bootstrapnode_reservation_id: ID of the Blazar reservation for the bootstrap node.
network_name: Name of the network.
image_name: Name of the image to be used by the cluster. Must be one of the following: Ubuntu22.04-HPC-MPI-Spack, Ubuntu22.04-HPC-MPI-Spack-CUDA, or Ubuntu22.04-HPC-MPI-Spack-ROCm. Defaults to Ubuntu22.04-HPC-MPI-Spack.
worker_count: Number of worker nodes. Defaults to 1.
spack_packages: List of additional Spack packages to install.
private_key_content: Contents of the SSH private key.
public_key_content: Contents of the SSH public key, allowing login into instances.
The following outputs are provided:

master_ip: Floating IP of the master node.
keypair_name: Name of the MPI keypair used.
You can create the stack using the following OpenStack CLI command:

SSH_KEY=/work/.ssh/id_rsa    # Path to the SSH key file that will be used as the cluster's keypair
STACK_NAME=mpi-stack
NETWORK_NAME=sharednet1
IMAGE_NAME=Ubuntu22.04-HPC-MPI-Spack
RESERVATION_ID=""            # Enter the reservation id
BOOTSTRAP_RESERVATION_ID=""  # Enter the bootstrap reservation id
WORKER_COUNT=1              # Number of worker nodes
SPACK_PACKAGES="pdsh,zlib"  # Comma-separated list of extra spack packages to be installed on all nodes

Create the stack
openstack stack create ${STACK_NAME} -t template.yml --wait \
    --parameter-file private_key_content=${SSH_KEY} \
    --parameter-file public_key_content=${SSH_KEY}.pub \
    --parameter network_name=${NETWORK_NAME} \
    --parameter image_name=${IMAGE_NAME} \
    --parameter bootstrapnode_reservation_id=${BOOTSTRAP_RESERVATION_ID} \
    --parameter reservation_id=${RESERVATION_ID} \
    --parameter worker_count=${WORKER_COUNT} \
    --parameter spack_packages=${SPACK_PACKAGES}


ansible MPI MPICH openmpi

parameters:
  bootstrapnode_reservation_id:
    type: string
    description: ID of the Blazar reservation for bootstrap node
    constraints:
      - custom_constraint: blazar.reservation

  reservation_id:
    type: string
    description: ID of the Blazar reservation for master/workers
    constraints:
      - custom_constraint: blazar.reservation

  network_name:
    type: string
    description: Network name (should be an existing one eg.sharednet1)
    constraints:
      - custom_constraint: neutron.network

  image_name:
    type: string
    description: Image Name to be used by the cluster
    default: Ubuntu22.04-HPC-MPI-Spack

  worker_count:
    type: number
    description: Number of worker nodes
    default: 1

  spack_packages:
    type: comma_delimited_list
    description: List of Spack packages to install
    default: [ pdsh ]

  private_key_content:
    type: string
    description: SSH private key contents

  public_key_content:
    type: string
    description: SSH public key content, allows logging into instances
 
  nfs_share_size:
    type: number
    description: Size of the NFS Share(nfs_mpi_share) which will be mounted at /nfs 
    default: 0
    constraints:
      - range: { min: 0 }

conditions:
  create_nfs_share: { not: { equals: [ { get_param: nfs_share_size }, 0 ] } }

resources:
  mpi_keypair:
    type: OS::Nova::KeyPair
    properties:
      name:
        list_join:
          - '-'
          - - { get_param: OS::stack_name }
            - keypair
      public_key: { get_param: public_key_content }

  bootstrap_node:
    type: OS::Nova::Server
    properties:
      name: mpi-bootstrap
      flavor: baremetal
      image: Ubuntu22.04-HPC-MPI-Spack
      key_name: { get_resource: mpi_keypair }
      networks:
        - network: sharednet1
      scheduler_hints: { reservation: { get_param: bootstrapnode_reservation_id } }
      user_data_format: RAW
      user_data:
        str_replace:
          template: |
            #!/bin/bash
            set -e

            mkdir -p /work/.ssh
            chown cc:cc /work/.ssh
            chmod 700 /work/.ssh

            cat > /work/.ssh/id_rsa <<EOF
            PRIVATE_KEY
            EOF

            cat > /work/.ssh/id_rsa.pub <<EOF
            PUBLIC_KEY
            EOF

            chmod 600 /work/.ssh/id_rsa
            chmod 644 /work/.ssh/id_rsa.pub
            chown -R cc:cc /work/.ssh

            apt-get update
            apt-get install -y git ansible

            cd /home/cc
            git clone https://github.com/pmodels/cc-hpc-appliances.git mpi-ansible
            cd mpi-ansible

            cat > inventory.ini <<EOF
            [master_node]
            MASTER_NAME ansible_host=MASTER_IP

            [worker_nodes]
            EOF

            IFS=',' read -r -a NAMES <<< "WORKER_NAMES"
            IFS=',' read -r -a IPS <<< "WORKER_IPS"
            for i in "${!NAMES[@]}"; do
              echo "${NAMES[$i]} ansible_host=${IPS[$i]}" >> inventory.ini
            done

            cat >> inventory.ini <<EOF
            [worker_nodes:vars]
            ansible_ssh_common_args='-o ProxyJump=cc@MASTER_IP'
            EOF
                        
            if [ -n "NFS_SHARE" ]; then
                EXPORT=$(echo "NFS_SHARE" | sed "s/[][]//g" | sed "s/'//g")
                NFS_LIST="[{'mount':'/nfs','export':'$EXPORT'}]"        
            else
                NFS_LIST="[]"
            fi
                        
            export ANSIBLE_PYTHON_INTERPRETER=/usr/bin/python3
            export ANSIBLE_SSH_ARGS="-F /home/cc/mpi-ansible/config"
            
            ansible-playbook -i ./inventory.ini -e "spack_packages=['SPACK_PACKAGES']" -e "nfs_shares='$NFS_LIST'" ./mpi-cluster.yml

          params:
            MASTER_NAME: { get_attr: [ master_node, name ] }
            MASTER_IP: { get_attr: [ master_floating_ip, ip ] }
            WORKER_NAMES: { list_join: [ ",", { get_attr: [ worker_nodes, name ] } ] }
            WORKER_IPS: { list_join: [ ",", { get_attr: [ worker_nodes, first_address ] } ] }
            PUBLIC_KEY: { get_param: public_key_content }
            PRIVATE_KEY: { get_param: private_key_content }
            SPACK_PACKAGES: { list_join: [ "','", { get_param: spack_packages } ] }
            NFS_SHARE:
              if:
                - create_nfs_share
                - { get_attr: [ nfs_share, export_locations ] }
                - ""

  master_node:
    type: OS::Nova::Server
    properties:
      name: mpi-master-node
      flavor: baremetal
      image: { get_param: image_name }
      key_name: { get_resource: mpi_keypair }
      networks:
        - network: { get_param: network_name }
      scheduler_hints: { reservation: { get_param: reservation_id } }

  worker_nodes:
    type: OS::Heat::ResourceGroup
    properties:
      count: { get_param: worker_count }
      resource_def:
        type: OS::Nova::Server
        properties:
          name: mpi-worker-node-%index%
          flavor: baremetal
          image: { get_param: image_name }
          key_name: { get_resource: mpi_keypair }
          networks:
            - network: { get_param: network_name }
          scheduler_hints: { reservation: { get_param: reservation_id } }

  nfs_share:
    type: OS::Manila::Share
    condition: create_nfs_share
    properties:
      name: mpi_nfs_share
      share_protocol: NFS
      size: { get_param: nfs_share_size }

  master_floating_ip:
    type: OS::Nova::FloatingIP
    properties:
      pool: public

  master_floating_ip_association:
    type: OS::Nova::FloatingIPAssociation
    properties:
      floating_ip: { get_resource: master_floating_ip }
      server_id: { get_resource: master_node }

outputs:
  master_ip:
    description: Floating IP of the Master node
    value: { get_attr: [ master_floating_ip, ip ] }

  keypair_name:
    description: Name of the MPI KeyPair used
    value: { get_resource: mpi_keypair }

title: MPI and Spack for HPC (Ubuntu 22.04)
short_description: This appliance is built on top of Ubuntu 22.04 and comes preconfigured with Spack for flexible software management, along with Lmod (Lua Modules).
long_description:
This appliance is built on top of Ubuntu 22.04 and comes preconfigured with [Spack](https://spack.io/) for flexible software management, along with [Lmod (Lua Modules)](https://lmod.readthedocs.io/en/latest/). Both MPICH and OpenMPI are installed and can be easily managed using module commands. You can use the module load and module unload commands to manage software packages for your HPC work.

To load MPICH, run:

module load mpich
You can confirm that the module is loaded by checking the list of currently loaded modules:

module list
You can now run MPI programs using MPICH. Here's a simple example program to compute the value of pi using numerical integration:

wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pmodels/mpich/master/examples/cpi.c
mpicc -o cpi cpi.c
mpiexec -n 4 ./cpi
Output should look something like:

Process 0 of 4 is on mpich.novalocal
Process 1 of 4 is on mpich.novalocal
Process 2 of 4 is on mpich.novalocal
Process 3 of 4 is on mpich.novalocal
pi is approximately 3.1415926544231239, Error is 0.0000000008333307
wall clock time = 0.000059
If you want to install a new package using Spack, use the following command:

spack install <package-name>

MPI MPICH Spack

title: MPI and Spack for HPC (Ubuntu 22.04 - CUDA)
short_description: This appliance is built on top of Ubuntu 22.04 and comes preconfigured with CUDA 12.8 and the NVIDIA driver version 575 for GPU-accelerated computing.
long_description:
This appliance is built on top of Ubuntu 22.04 and comes preconfigured with CUDA 12.8 and the NVIDIA driver version 575 for GPU-accelerated computing. It also includes Spack for flexible software management and Lmod (Lua Modules). Both MPICH and OpenMPI are installed and can be easily managed using module commands. You can use the module load and module unload commands to manage software packages for your HPC workloads.

To load MPICH, run:

module load mpich
The loaded MPICH is already installed with CUDA support.

You can now run CUDA-MPI programs using MPICH. Here's a simple example program:

wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pmodels/mpich/master/examples/cuda/cudapi.cu
nvcc -ccbin mpicxx -o cudapi cudapi.cu
mpirun -np 4 ./cudapi
If you want to install a new package using Spack. Use the +cuda variant to enable CUDA support during installation:

spack install <package-name> +cuda    # Enables CUDA support

cuda MPI MPICH Spack

title: MPI and Spack for HPC (Ubuntu 22.04 - ROCm)
short_description: This appliance is built on top of Ubuntu 22.04 and comes configured with ROCm 6.4.2 for GPU-accelerated computing.
long_description:
This appliance is built on top of Ubuntu 22.04 and comes configured with ROCm 6.4.2 for GPU-accelerated computing. It also includes Spack for flexible software management and Lmod (Lua Modules). Both MPICH and OpenMPI are installed and can be easily managed using module commands. You can use the module load and module unload commands to manage software packages for your HPC workloads.

To load OpenMPI, run:

module load openmpi
The loaded OpenMPI is already installed with rocm support.

You can now compile and run ROCm-MPI programs using HIP. For example:

export OMPI_CC=hipcc
mpicc -o ./hello ./hello.cpp
mpirun -n 3 ./hello
If you want to install a new package using Spack. Use the +rocm variant to enable ROCm support during installation:

spack install <package-name> +rocm    # Enables ROCm support

title: MPI + SR-IOV KVM cluster
short_description: This appliance deploys an MPI cluster of KVM virtual machines using the MVAPICH2-Virt implementation and configured with SR-IOV for high-performance communication over InfiniBand.
long_description:
This appliance deploys an MPI cluster of KVM virtual machines using the MVAPICH2-Virt implementation and configured with SR-IOV for high-performance communication over InfiniBand.

[User guide](https://mvapich.cse.ohio-state.edu/userguide/virt/)

It accepts the following parameters:

key_name: name of a key pair to enable SSH access to the instance (defaults to "default")
reservation_id: ID of the Blazar reservation to use for launching instances
total_nodes: Number of physical nodes to launch
total_vms: Number of virtual machines to create
vcpu_per_vm: Number of VCPUs per virtual machine
memory_per_vm: Amount of memory size per virtual machine (in GiB)
The following outputs are provided:

first_instance_ip: The public IP address of the first bare-metal instance. Login with the command 'ssh cc@first_instance_ip'.
To check the VM / IP mapping list, run the following command:

cat /home/cc/vm-ip_mapping.dat
To run an MPI program, first login to one VM using command "ssh root@vm_ip", then execute the following command, assuming you have compiled a program called mpi.out:

mpirun_rsh -np <nprocs> -hostfile vmhosts MV2_VIRT_USE_IVSHMEM=1 ./mpi.out
In some cases, the library path of the MVAPICH2-Virt package needs to be exported as follows before running MPI programs:

export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/mvapich2-virt/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
Refer to the MVAPICH2-Virt user guide for more details on running MPI programs.


MVAPICH2-Virt SR-IOV

authors.affiliation: Network Based Computing Lab, The Ohio State University

environment_setup.arguments:
heat_template_version: 2015-10-15

description: MPI cluster using KVM + SR-IOV and the MVAPICH2-Virt library. 
             Please make sure that you have leased a set of nodes with InfiniBand
             support before launching this complex appliance.

parameters:

    type: string
    label: Key name
    description: Name of a key pair to enable SSH access to the instance
    default: default
    constraints:
    - custom_constraint: nova.keypair
  reservation_id:
    type: string

    constraints:
    - custom_constraint: blazar.reservation

  total_nodes:
    type: number

    default: 1
    constraints:

  total_vms:

resources:
  mpi_keypair:
    type: OS::Nova::KeyPair
    properties:
      save_private_key: true
      name:
        str_replace:
          template: mpi_stack_id
          params:
            stack_id: { get_param: "OS::stack_id" }

  instance_floating_ip:
    type: OS::Nova::FloatingIP
    properties:
      pool: public

  ports:
    type: OS::Heat::ResourceGroup
    properties:
      count: { get_param: total_vms }
      resource_def:
        type: OS::Neutron::Port
        properties:
          name: my-port-%index%
          network: sharednet1

  instance_association:
    type: OS::Nova::FloatingIPAssociation
    properties:
      floating_ip: { get_resource: instance_floating_ip }
      server_id: { get_attr: [mpi_cluster, resource.0] }

  mpi_cluster:
    type: OS::Heat::ResourceGroup
    properties:
      count: { get_param: total_nodes }
      resource_def:
        type: OS::Nova::Server
        properties:
          name: mpi-instance-%index%
          image: DIB-OSU-CentOS7-SRIOV-MVAPICH2-Virt
          flavor: baremetal
          key_name: { get_param: key_name }
          networks:
             - network: sharednet1
          scheduler_hints: { reservation: { get_param: reservation_id } }

          user_data:
            str_replace:
              template: |
                #!/bin/bash
                phyname=`hostname`
                instance_name=`echo $phyname | cut -d '-' -f 1`
                instance_index=`echo $phyname | cut -d '-' -f 3`
                # disable HT
                for CPU in `seq 24 47`
                do
                   echo "0" > /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu$CPU/online;
                done
                sudo yum -y install uuid wget

                # Take care of access key for instance and VM
                cd /home/cc/.ssh/
                cat << EOF > id_rsa.pub
                public_key
                EOF
                cat << EOF > id_rsa
                private_key
                EOF
                cat << EOF > config
                Host *
                  StrictHostKeyChecking no
                EOF
                cat id_rsa.pub >> authorized_keys
                chmod 600 authorized_keys id_rsa
                chmod 644 id_rsa.pub config
                sudo /bin/bash -c "cp /home/cc/.ssh/id_rsa /home/cc/.ssh/id_rsa.pub /home/cc/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/cc/.ssh/config /root/.ssh/"
                sudo guestfish add /home/cc/chameleon-mvapich2-virt-appliance.qcow2 : run : mount /dev/sda1 / : upload /home/cc/.ssh/id_rsa /root/.ssh/id_rsa 2>&1 | tee -a /home/cc/stack.log
                sudo guestfish add /home/cc/chameleon-mvapich2-virt-appliance.qcow2 : run : mount /dev/sda1 / : upload /home/cc/.ssh/id_rsa.pub /root/.ssh/id_rsa.pub 2>&1 | tee -a /home/cc/stack.log
                sudo guestfish add /home/cc/chameleon-mvapich2-virt-appliance.qcow2 : run : mount /dev/sda1 / : upload /home/cc/.ssh/authorized_keys /root/.ssh/authorized_keys 2>&1 | tee -a /home/cc/stack.log
                sudo guestfish add /home/cc/chameleon-mvapich2-virt-appliance.qcow2 : run : mount /dev/sda1 / : upload /home/cc/.ssh/config /root/.ssh/config 2>&1 | tee -a /home/cc/stack.log
                sudo chown cc:cc *

                # Save VM/IP mapping list in instance
                cd /home/cc/
                vm_per_node=$(( total_vms / total_nodes ))
                for j in `seq 0 $((total_vms - 1))`
                do
                    node_index=$(( $j / $vm_per_node ))
                    modulo=$(( $j % $vm_per_node ))
                    vmip=`echo port_ips | cut -d ',' -f $(( $j + 1 )) | sed -e 's/ //g'`
                    item="$vmip ${instance_name}-instance-${node_index}-vm-${modulo}"
                    echo $item >> /home/cc/vm-ip_mapping.dat
                    sudo /bin/bash -c "echo $item >> /etc/hosts"
                done
                cat /home/cc/vm-ip_mapping.dat | awk '{print $2}' >> /home/cc/vmhosts

                # Insert VM/IP mapping list into /etc/hosts in VM image
                # Use upload as \newline does not work in write-append
                # Might need a decent way
                echo "127.0.0.1 localhost localhost.localdomain localhost4 localhost4.localdomain4" >> localfile
                echo "::1  localhost localhost.localdomain localhost4 localhost4.localdomain4" >> localfile
                cat /home/cc/vm-ip_mapping.dat >> localfile
                sudo guestfish add chameleon-mvapich2-virt-appliance.qcow2 : run : mount /dev/sda1 / : upload localfile /etc/hosts
                rm -f localfile

                # Upload MV2-vm installation script and vmhosts in VM image
                sudo guestfish add /home/cc/chameleon-mvapich2-virt-appliance.qcow2 : run : mount /dev/sda1 / : upload /root/mv2-chameleon-vm.sh /root/mv2-chameleon-vm.sh 2>&1 | tee -a /home/cc/stack.log
                sudo guestfish add /home/cc/chameleon-mvapich2-virt-appliance.qcow2 : run : mount /dev/sda1 / : upload /home/cc/vmhosts /root/vmhosts 2>&1 | tee -a /home/cc/stack.log

                # Launch and setup VMs
                wget https://go.osu.edu/mv2-virt-chameleon-template -O template.xml
                for i in `seq 0 $(($vm_per_node - 1))`
                do
                    vm_index=$(( $instance_index * $vm_per_node + $i + 1 ))
                    vm_mac=`echo port_macs | cut -d ',' -f $vm_index | sed -e 's/ //g'`
                    vm_ip=`echo port_ips | cut -d ',' -f $vm_index | sed -e 's/ //g'`

                    uuid=`uuidgen`
                    echo $i $uuid 2>&1 | tee -a /home/cc/stack.log
                    qemu-img create -b chameleon-mvapich2-virt-appliance.qcow2 -f qcow2 vm-$i.disk

                    cp /home/cc/template.xml /home/cc/$phyname-vm-$i.xml
                    sed -i s/@instance/$phyname-vm-$i/ /home/cc/$phyname-vm-$i.xml
                    sed -i s/@uuid/$uuid/ /home/cc/$phyname-vm-$i.xml
                    sed -i s/@memory/memory_per_vm/ /home/cc/$phyname-vm-$i.xml
                    sed -i s/@vcpu/vcpu_per_vm/ /home/cc/$phyname-vm-$i.xml
                    sed -i s/@n/$i/ /home/cc/$phyname-vm-$i.xml
                    sed -i s/@mac/$vm_mac/ /home/cc/$phyname-vm-$i.xml

                    sudo virsh create /home/cc/$phyname-vm-$i.xml 2>&1 | tee -a /home/cc/stack.log

                    while ! sudo grep -q "$vm_ip" /home/cc/console-vm$i.log
                    do
                       sleep 2
                    done
                    cat /home/cc/console-vm$i.log | grep "$vm_ip" | tee -a /home/cc/stack.log

                    sudo virsh qemu-monitor-command $phyname-vm-$i --pretty '{"execute":"device_add","arguments":{"driver":"ivshmem", "id":"hpivshmem","shm":"ivs","size":"256m"}}'
                    ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no root@$vm_ip hostname $phyname-vm-${i} 2>&1 | tee -a /home/cc/download.log
                    ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no root@$vm_ip chmod 600 /root/.ssh/id_rsa 2>&1 | tee -a /home/cc/download.log
                done

              params:
                total_nodes: { get_param: total_nodes }
                private_key: { get_attr: [ mpi_keypair, private_key ] }
                public_key: { get_attr: [ mpi_keypair, public_key ] }
                total_vms: { get_param: total_vms }
                vcpu_per_vm: { get_param: vcpu_per_vm }
                memory_per_vm: { get_param: memory_per_vm }
                port_macs: { list_join: [', ', {get_attr: [ports, mac_address]} ] }
                port_ips: { list_join: [', ', {get_attr: [ports, fixed_ips, 0, ip_address]} ] }


outputs:
    first_instance_ip:
      description: The public IP address of the first bare-metal instance. Login with the command 'ssh cc@first_instance_ip'.
      value: { get_attr: [instance_floating_ip, ip] }

title: Large Data Flow Appliance
short_description: It is important to provide researchers with support for experiments requiring large data flows, including high-performance data movement in experimental cloud environments.
long_description:
Description
It is important to provide researchers with support for experiments requiring large data flows, including high-performance data movement in experimental cloud environments. This support involves tuning many different components to achieve a high-performance system. Often, it is the case that learning, setting up, and tuning the system and tools takes the majority of the time for experimenters. Providing a pre-tuned environment, tools for experiments, and reference performance results for researchers would assist them to be more productive. This Appliance helps users to build a set of compute nodes to test a large data flow network application between multiple DTNs.

For how to use this appliance, please refer to the documentation.

[Documentation](https://www.chameleoncloud.org/appliances/50/docs/)

Design
8-DTNs 

Each stack of the appliance consists of multiple DTNs connected in a user-defined network. Each DTN is fine-tuned for large data flow application, fully utilizing the available network capacity. It comes with multiple tools to test the network and disk performance of the DTN. Users can test each DTN within an appliance or spawn multiple stacks of the appliance to test between them.

Requirement
For each stack of the appliance, minimum of 5 bare-metal compute node need to be available in an active reservation.

Also, the user needs to specify the network that the DTNs will be connected to.

What's available?
Each DTN comes with an Ubuntu 16.04 node with network stack optimization for 10 Gbps. It comes with network testing tool such as iperf, iperf3 and nuttcp and disk testing tool, fio.

In addition to the tools, Chameleon Large Flow Tester is included to test between each DTN. It automates network test and disk test end to end and allow users to emulate arbitrary network environments, such as delay, jitter, and loss rate.

Heat Template
Heat Template requires few inputs from the user at the time of stack creation.

Key pair for the Chameleon Cloud.

Reservation ID with at least 5 available bare-metal nodes.

Network ID for attaching the DTNs to.

After the stack is spawned, it outputs

Internal IP address of each DTN in the specified network.

Internal IP address of the Head node (Access node to other DTN) in the specified network.

Floating IP address of the Head node the user can ssh into.

environment_setup.arguments:
# This describes what is deployed by this template.
description: Hadoop master and workers deployed with Heat on Chameleon

# This defines the minimum Heat version required by this template.

# The resources section defines what OpenStack resources are to be deployed and

resources:
  router_to_ext:
    type: OS::Neutron::Router
    properties:
      name: hadoop_router
      external_gateway_info:
        network: public

  hadoop_subnet:
    type: OS::Neutron::Subnet
    properties:
      name: hadoop_subnet
      cidr: { get_param: network_cidr }
      enable_dhcp: true
      network: { get_resource: hadoop_network }

  hadoop_network:
    type: OS::Neutron::Net

  hadoop_router_interface:
    type: OS::Neutron::RouterInterface
    properties:
      router: { get_resource: router_to_ext }
      subnet: { get_resource: hadoop_subnet }




  hadoop_master_floating_ip:
    type: OS::Nova::FloatingIP
    properties:
      pool: public

  hadoop_workers:
    type: OS::Heat::ResourceGroup
    properties:
      count: { get_param: hadoop_worker_count }
      resource_def:
        type: OS::Nova::Server
        properties:
          name: worker-%index%
          flavor: baremetal
          image: CC-CentOS7
          key_name: { get_param: key_name }
          networks:
             - network: { get_resource: hadoop_network }
          scheduler_hints: { reservation: { get_param: reservation_id } }
          user_data:
            str_replace:
              template: |
                #!/bin/bash
                echo nameserver 8.8.8.8 >> /etc/resolv.conf   
                wget http://geni-images.renci.org/images/tutorials/Chameleon-hadoop/hadoop_config_worker.sh
                chmod +x hadoop_config_worker.sh
                ./hadoop_config_worker.sh >> /tmp/boot.log 2>&1
              params:
                $worker_count: { get_param: hadoop_worker_count }

  hadoop_master:
    type: OS::Nova::Server
    properties:
      name: master
      flavor: baremetal
      image: CC-CentOS7
      key_name: { get_param: key_name }
      networks:
         - network: { get_resource: hadoop_network }
      scheduler_hints: { reservation: { get_param: reservation_id } }
      user_data:
        str_replace:
          template: |
            #!/bin/bash
            echo nameserver 8.8.8.8 >> /etc/resolv.conf 
            wget http://geni-images.renci.org/images/tutorials/Chameleon-hadoop/hadoop_config_master.sh
            chmod +x hadoop_config_master.sh
            
            echo $worker_ips > /tmp/client_ips.txt
            echo $worker_names > /tmp/client_names.txt

          params:

    properties:

      server_id: { get_resource: hadoop_master }

short_description: This template deploys an Ansible cluster on baremetal sites. It deploys a head node with Ansible installed, and x worker nodes which are configurable through Ansible.
long_description:
[Appliance Documentation](https://chameleoncloud.org/appliances/106/docs/)
This template deploys an Ansible cluster on baremetal sites. It deploys a head node with Ansible installed, and x worker nodes which are configurable through Ansible.

Users can use this Ansible cluster to manage their application deployments and configuration management.

It has been tested on CentOS7 and may need some adjustments for other distributions.

Requirements:
- Tested on CC-CentOS7
- Reservation with min 2 compute nodes like haswell, skylake, cascadelake_r

Launch inputs:
- Image name (CentOS7)
- Key name: A keypair to access the head node. A different keypair 'ansible-worker-key' is created for the workers. Workers can be accessed by ssh through the head node. - Num workers: How many workers to launch in addition to the head node, minimum 1
- Reservation id: The reservation for the lease created - Network: Network name to launch on

Outputs:
- 1 head node with Ansible installed
Installation directory: /etc/ansible
Inventory: /home/cc/inventory - 1 or more worker nodes reachable over ssh from the head node

To test cluster:

$ ansible -i /home/cc/inventory all -m shell -a "hostname"

Ansible commands can be executed with the 'cc' user, using 'become' privilege escalation when needed.

Ansible user documentation:
https://docs.ansible.com/ansible/latest/user_guide/index.html

title: UBGen
short_description: UBGen is an automated UB program genertor for C
long_description:
UBGen is an automated UB program genertor for C. Given a valid C program, UBGen can mutate it to generate programs containing undefined behaviors. For each of the generated UB program, it only contains one kind of undefined behavior at one program location.

UBGen is designed in our research paper "UBfuzz: Finding Bugs in Sanitizer Implementations" (ASPLOS 2024), where UBGen is the program generator for UBfuzz. For the full evaluation of UBfuzz, please find the artifact as stated in the paper.

title: Zorse: Efficient LLM Training on Heterogeneous GPU Clusters
short_description: Efficient LLM Training on Heterogeneous GPU Clusters
long_description: Zorse is a system for efficient LLM training on heterogeneous GPU clusters. It uses Pipeline-Efficient ZeRO DP, a novel integration of pipeline parallelism and data parallelism that is both communication- and memory-efficient. This Trovi artifact demonstrates running Zorse on a Chameleon Cloud bare-metal V100 node, walking through profiling, planning, and training end-to-end.

title: FlexProf: Flexible, Side-Channel-Free Memory Access
short_description: FlexProf is a side-channel-free memory scheduler that uses profiling-guided read/write modes to improve secure multi-tenant performance, achieving up to 33% speedup over prior defenses.
long_description: Memory controllers in multi-tenant systems can leak sensitive information through timing-based side channels. Prior secure schedulers prevent leakage but often reduce performance due to rigid worst-case timing constraints. FlexProf introduces a flexible, profiling-guided scheduling approach that alternates between read- and write-optimized modes while remaining deterministic and secure. This design preserves security guarantees and improves performance by up to 33% over previous leakage-free solutions.

The following tutorial aims to provide a series of examples on how to use the [Raspberry Pi Sense Hat](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/accessories/sense-hat.html) and the [Waveshare sense hat's (B)](https://www.waveshare.com/wiki/Sense_HAT_(B)#Product_PK) onboard sensors to record various metrics about the environment on CHI@Edge-hosted Raspberry Pi devices.

   * Jupyter notebook showcasing how to read values using each of the sensors using [AdaFruit Blinka and CircuitPython libraries](https://learn.adafruit.com/welcome-to-circuitpython/what-is-circuitpython), and example scripts that use them.
   * Readme with more in-depth information about how this device was set up behind the scenes to accommodate sense hat support. 

This artifact is maintained on a best-effort basis by our support team, contributions to this peripheral support or any peripheral support on CHI@Edge are highly welcome. 

We encourage our users to visit the newly updated official [documentation](https://chameleoncloud.gitbook.io/chi-edge/device-enrollment/peripherals-and-device-profiles) on how to enable peripherals on CHI@Edge devices.

Happy sensing!

title: BIDL: A High-throughput, Low-latency Permissioned Blockchain Framework for Datacenter Networks
short_description:
Source: dl.acm.org

Link: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3477132.3483574

Conference: sosp2021

A permissioned blockchain framework typically runs an efficient Byzantine consensus protocol and is attr
long_description:
Source: dl.acm.org

Link: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3477132.3483574

Conference: sosp2021

A permissioned blockchain framework typically runs an efficient Byzantine consensus protocol and is attractive to deploy fast trading applications among a large number of mutually untrusted participants (e.g., companies). Unfortunately, all existing permissioned blockchain frameworks adopt sequential workflows for invoking the consensus protocol and executing applications' transactions, making the performance of these applications much lower than deploying them in traditional systems (e.g., in-datacenter stock exchange).

We propose Bidl, the first permissioned blockchain framework highly optimized for datacenter networks. We leverage the network ordering in such networks to create a shepherded parallel workflow, which carries a sequencer to parallelize the consensus protocol and transaction execution speculatively. However, the presence of malicious participants (e.g., a malicious sequencer) can easily perturb the parallel workflow to greatly degrade Bidl's performance. To achieve stable high performance, Bidl efficiently shepherds all participants by detecting their misbehaviors, and performs denylist-based view changes to replace or deny malicious participants. Compared with three fast permissioned blockchain frameworks, Bidl's parallel workflow reduces applications' latency by up to 72.7% and improves their throughput by up to 4.3x in the presence of malicious participants. Bidl is suitable to be integrated with traditional stock exchange systems. Bidl's code is released on github.com/hku-systems/bidl.

title: NFS share
short_description: This appliance deploys an NFS server with a configurable number of clients.
long_description:
This appliance deploys an NFS server with a configurable number of clients. The NFS server creates a directory at /exports/example, changes its ownership to the "cc" user and group, and exports it. The NFS clients add this NFS share to /etc/fstab and mount it.

This appliance accepts the following parameters:

nfs_client_count: Number of NFS client instances (defaults to 1)
key_name: name of a key pair to enable SSH access to the instance (defaults to "default")
reservation_id: ID of the Blazar reservation to use for launching instances
The following outputs are provided:

server_ip: the public IP address of the NFS server
client_ips: the private IP addresses of the NFS clients

environment_setup.arguments:
# This describes what is deployed by this template.
description: NFS server and clients deployed with Heat on Chameleon

# This defines the minimum Heat version required by this template.
heat_template_version: 2015-10-15

# The resources section defines what OpenStack resources are to be deployed and
# how they should be configured.
resources:
  nfs_server_floating_ip:
    type: OS::Nova::FloatingIP
    properties:
      pool: public

  nfs_server:
    type: OS::Nova::Server
    properties:
      flavor: baremetal
      image: CC-CentOS7
      key_name: { get_param: key_name }
      networks:
         - network: sharednet1
      scheduler_hints: { reservation: { get_param: reservation_id } }
      user_data: |
        #!/bin/bash
        yum install -y nfs-utils
        mkdir -p /exports/example
        chown -R cc:cc /exports
        echo '/exports/example 10.0.0.0/8(rw,async)' >> /etc/exports
        systemctl enable rpcbind && systemctl start rpcbind
        systemctl enable nfs-server && systemctl start nfs-server

  nfs_server_ip_association:
    type: OS::Nova::FloatingIPAssociation
    properties:
      floating_ip: { get_resource: nfs_server_floating_ip }
      server_id: { get_resource: nfs_server }

  nfs_clients:
    type: OS::Heat::ResourceGroup
    properties:
      count: { get_param: nfs_client_count }
      resource_def:
        type: OS::Nova::Server
        properties:
          flavor: baremetal
          image: CC-CentOS7
          key_name: { get_param: key_name }
          networks:
             - network: sharednet1
          scheduler_hints: { reservation: { get_param: reservation_id } }
          user_data:
            str_replace:
              template: |
                #!/bin/bash
                yum install -y nfs-utils
                echo "$nfs_server_ip:/exports/example    /mnt/    nfs" > /etc/fstab
                mount -a
              params:
                $nfs_server_ip: { get_attr: [nfs_server, first_address] }

# The parameters section gathers configuration from the user.
parameters:
  nfs_client_count:
    type: number
    description: Number of NFS client instances
    default: 1
    constraints:
      - range: { min: 1 }
        description: There must be at least one client.
  key_name:
    type: string
    description: Name of a KeyPair to enable SSH access to the instance
    default: default
    constraints:
    - custom_constraint: nova.keypair
  reservation_id:
    type: string
    description: ID of the Blazar reservation to use for launching instances.
    constraints:
    - custom_constraint: blazar.reservation

outputs:
  server_ip:
    description: Public IP address of the NFS server
    value: { get_attr: [nfs_server_floating_ip, ip] }
  client_ips:
    description: Private IP addresses of the NFS clients
    value: { get_attr: [nfs_clients, first_address] }

title: Large-scale model training on Chameleon (H100 version)
short_description: Fine-tune a LLM across multiple GPUs on Chameleon.
long_description:
In this tutorial, we practice fine-tuning a large language model. We will use a selection of techniques to allow us to train models that would not otherwise fit in GPU memory:

* gradient accumulation
* reduced precision
* activation checkpointing
* CPU offload
* parameter efficient fine tuning
* distributed training across multiple GPUs 

Follow along at [Large-scale model training on Chameleon](https://teaching-on-testbeds.github.io/llm-chi/index_h100).

This lab has two parts:

* `single/`: single-GPU large-model training, requires an A100 80GB or H100 GPU
* `multi/`: multi-GPU large-model training, requires a 4x A100 80GB or 4x H100 GPU

There is an A100 version of this artifact and an H100 version of this artifact, tuned for different GPUs; this is the H100 version. Refer to the related artifacts for the A100 version.

---

title: Data platforms on Chameleon
short_description: Data engineering! PostgreSQL, RedPanda, Airflow, and Iceberg
long_description:
This lab builds a small data platform for a hypothetical GourmetGram service:

* use PostgreSQL for application data
* Support real time event services with RedPanda
* materialize Iceberg tables with Airflow

title: ICSE 2024: FPLearner
short_description: Predicting Performance and Accuracy of Mixed-Precision Programs for Precision Tuning
long_description: A mixed-precision program is a floating-point program that utilizes different precisions for different operations, providing the opportunity of balancing the trade-off between accuracy and performance. Precision tuning aims to find a mixed-precision version of a program that improves its performance while maintaining a given accuracy. Unfortunately, existing precision tuning approaches are either limited to small-scale programs, or suffer from efficiency issues. In this paper, we propose FPLearner, a novel approach that addresses these limitations. Our insight is to leverage a Machine Learning based technique, Graph Neural Networks, to learn the representation of mixed-precision programs to predict their performance and accuracy. Such prediction models can then be used to accelerate the process of dynamic precision tuning by reducing the number of program runs. We create a dataset of mixed-precision programs from five diverse HPC applications for training our models, which achieve 96.34% F1 score in performance prediction and 97.03% F1 score in accuracy prediction. FPLearner improves the time efficiency of two dynamic precision tuners, Precimoniousand HiFPTuner, by an average of 25.54% and up to 61.07% while achieving precision tuning results of comparable or better quality.

title: Build an MLOps Pipeline
short_description: Automate system deployment and application lifecycle management with an MLOps pipeline on Chameleon
long_description:
In [Cloud Computing on Chameleon](https://teaching-on-testbeds.github.io/cloud-chi/), we deployed a basic machine learning service to an OpenStack cloud. However, that deployment involved a lot of manual steps ("ClickOps"), and any updates to it would similarly involve lots of manual effort, be difficult to track, etc.

In this tutorial, we will learn how to automate both the initial deployment, and updates during the lifecycle of the application. We will:

* practice deploying systems following infrastructure-as-code and configuration-as-code principles using automated deployment tools
* and create an automated pipeline to manage a machine learning model through its lifecycle 

Follow along at [Build an MLOps Pipeline](https://teaching-on-testbeds.github.io/mlops-chi/)!

Our experiment will use the following automated deployment and lifecycle management tools:

* Terraform: A declarative Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool used to provision and manage cloud infrastructure (servers, networks, etc.) by defining the desired end state in configuration files. Here, we use it to provision our infrastructure.
* Ansible: An imperative Configuration as Code (CaC) tool that automates system configuration, software installation, and application deployment through task-based YAML playbooks describing the steps to achieve a desired setup. Here, we use it to install Kubernetes and the Argo tools on our infrastructure after it is provisioned
* Argo CD: A declarative GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes that automatically syncs and deploys applications based on the desired state stored in Git repositories.
* Argo Workflows: A Kubernetes-native workflow engine where you define workflows, which execute tasks inside containers to run pipelines, jobs, or automation processes.

To run this experiment, you should have already created an account on Chameleon, and become part of a project. You should also have added your SSH key to the KVM@TACC site.

This tutorial uses: three `m1.large` VMs at KVM@TACC, and one floating IP.

During reproduction, we identified and fixed an implementation issue in the original code that prevented complete processing of the dataset. With the corrected code, we successfully reproduced the experiments and confirmed the paper's conclusion that BERT embeddings exhibit Row Order Insignificance.

This Jupyter notebook provides complete end-to-end reproduction on Chameleon Cloud GPU instances (RTX 6000), including infrastructure provisioning, environment setup, data acquisition from WikiTables dataset, running experiments with both original and corrected implementations, and statistical analysis. The workflow is fully documented and takes approximately 30 to 45 minutes to execute.

The artifact demonstrates transparent reproducibility research by documenting the complete reproduction process, including challenges encountered and solutions applied. All code, data processing steps, and analysis scripts are included, enabling others to verify our findings and build upon this work.

We executed the data analysis pipelines to evaluate the prevalence of open-source code (OSC) and its correlation with academic citations across three major research communities.

title: HeMem: Scalable Tiered Memory Management for Big Data Applications and Real NVM Reproducibility
short_description: Reproducibility of HeMem: Scalable Tiered Memory Management for Big Data Applications and Real NVM, SOSP, 2021.
long_description:
This artifact accompanies the SOSP 2021 paper “HeMem: Scalable Tiered Memory Management for Big Data Applications”.
HeMem is a tiered main-memory management system designed from scratch for systems with heterogeneous memory technologies (e.g., DRAM and persistent memory).

Unlike traditional page-table–based approaches, HeMem tracks memory access behavior using sampled CPU events and performs asynchronous, batched page migration. This design allows HeMem to scale to terabytes of memory while minimizing TLB shootdown and migration overheads. HeMem further exposes memory management policy at user level, enabling flexible per-application optimization.

title: Reproducing Gradient-GA for Sample-Efficient Molecular Optimization
short_description: Reproduced code and experimental results for Gradient-GA
long_description:
### **Overview**

This artifact reproduces the main experiments from the paper **Gradient GA: Gradient Genetic Algorithm For Drug Molecular Design**.

We reimplemented and executed the molecular optimization pipelines to evaluate Gradient-GA and multiple baseline methods under a fixed oracle-call budget.

**Includes:**
- **Reproduced Code:** Full codebase used to run Gradient-GA and baseline methods.
- **Experimental Results:** Raw outputs and aggregated statistics from our runs.
- **Analysis Scripts:** Scripts to compute AUC Top-1, Top-10, Top-100 and generate plots, heatmaps, and tables.
- **Original Paper:** Gradient GA: Gradient Genetic Algorithm For Drug Molecular Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09860 

**Reproduction Goal**

Validate the main claim of the paper that incorporating gradient information accelerates convergence in molecular optimization under a strict oracle-call budget.

**Key Findings (From my experiments)**

The reproduced experiments partially support the claims of the original paper. While Gradient-GA demonstrates competitive convergence behavior on certain objectives, its performance advantage is not consistently observed across all tasks and metrics. These results highlight both the potential and the limitations of incorporating gradient information into genetic molecular optimization frameworks.

**Environment and Notes**

- Python 3.9+
- PyTorch, NumPy, RDKit, TDC
- Fixed random seeds
- Minor modifications for reproducibility and consistent logging

title: LLM Benchmarks for Network Application with NetPress Reproducibility
short_description: This artifact is successfully reproduction on NetPress: Dynamically Generated LLM Benchmarks for Network Applications
long_description:
This artifact documents a personal reproduction attempt of the NetPress MALT benchmark framework for evaluating LLM agents on dynamic graph query tasks. The goal is to assess the practicality and robustness of the system under a constrained yet realistic cloud GPU environment while preserving the core evaluation logic of the original design.

Original Paper
NetPress: a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on graph-based system reasoning tasks, ArXiv 2025
Link: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.03231

Reproduction Goal
- The feasibility of running the benchmark with a reduced-scale local LLM backend
- The sensitivity of the system to backend and architectural choices
- The focus is on system fidelity and reproducibility rather than achieving peak performance.

Key Findings:
Pipeline Correctness
The MALT benchmark pipeline (dynamic query generation, LLM-based code synthesis, execution, and correctness evaluation) was successfully reproduced and executed end-to-end.

Deterministic Evaluation Behavior
Enforcing greedy decoding and fixed generation parameters yielded stable, reproducible outputs across runs, facilitating controlled benchmark evaluation.

Environment and Modifications
Environment: Cloud VM running Ubuntu 22.04
Hardware: Single NVIDIA RTX 6000 GPU

Critical Modifications:
- Migrated LLM backend from vLLM to HuggingFace Transformers for improved portability and device stability
- Replaced large-scale model configurations with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to fit single-GPU constraints
- Reorganized output directories to enable systematic comparison across model and prompt variants

Limitations
This reproduction does not claim performance parity with the original results, particularly regarding throughput and latency. The emphasis is on correctness, system behavior, and reproducibility under practical deployment constraints.

Conclusion
This reproduction demonstrates that the NetPress MALT benchmark remains functionally robust under a cloud-based single-GPU setup, while highlighting the sensitivity of LLM-based system benchmarks to backend assumptions and model scale choices.

title: Magneto-oracle suite for mobile app testing
short_description: This artifact reproduces experiments with the MAGNETO oracle suite for mobile app testing.
long_description:
Overview

- **Back Button:** Test failed (SSIM similarity very low, ~0.04 vs threshold 0.8).
- **Theme Change:** Theme change not detected, flagged as failure.

title: MISO reproduction attempt
short_description: MISO: Multi-Implicit-Submaps SLAM Reproduction
long_description:
This artifact provides a complete, end-to-end reproduction of the MISO SLAM system. MISO is designed for large-scale 3D reconstruction using implicit neural representations. Unlike global implicit methods, MISO breaks the environment into multiple submaps, allowing for better scalability and faster updates in dynamic or large-scale environments.

What this Experiment Does
This notebook automates the provisioning of high-performance Bare Metal hardware on Chameleon Cloud to perform the following:

Hardware Allocation: Provisions a GPU-enabled node (e.g., Tesla P100 or V100) required for neural implicit processing.

Environment Setup: Bootstraps a complex CUDA-accelerated Python environment, including PyTorch 1.13, PyTorch3D, and specialized 3D libraries like pysdf.

Data Acquisition: Automatically downloads and organizes the Newer College Dataset (NCD), specifically focusing on the "Quad" sequence.

Execution: Runs the full SLAM pipeline to generate a 3D mesh reconstruction from LiDAR/RGB-D data.

Output: Produces a .ply file representing the final reconstructed 3D environment.

Technical Requirements
To run this reproduction, the artifact requires:

Site: CHI@TACC or CHI@UC (where GPU nodes are available).

Node Type: gpu_p100 or gpu_v100.

Time to Run: Approximately 30–45 minutes (includes 10m for hardware boot, 10m for environment setup, and 15m for SLAM execution).

How to Reproduce
Launch: Click the "Launch on JupyterHub" button.

Configure: Open main (5).ipynb. Ensure your Chameleon Project Name is set correctly in the first cell.

Run All: Execute the cells in order. The notebook is designed to handle system locks and dependency conflicts automatically.

Visualize: Once the SLAM pipeline finishes, the notebook will download the final_reconstruction.ply file.

References
Original Paper: MISO: Multi-Implicit-Submaps for Large-Scale SLAM

Source Code: muhnatha/reproduce_MISO

Dataset: Newer College Dataset (Oxford Robotics Institute)

title: Reproduction of Building Verified Neural Networks for Computer Systems with Ouroboros from MLSys 2023
short_description: Reproduction of Ouroboros (MLSys 2023) validating spec-aware learning speedup on CPU.
long_description:
This artifact is a successful reproduction of the core performance claims from the paper "Building Verified Neural Networks for Computer Systems with Ouroboros" (MLSys 2023).

Original Paper: Building Verified Neural Networks for Computer Systems with Ouroboros, MLSys 2023. Link: https://proceedings.mlsys.org/paper_files/paper/2023/file/f025a252767e89e63426e42b4716d311-Paper-mlsys2023.pdf

Reproduction Goal:
The goal was to validate the relative performance gains of Ouroboros's spec-aware learning techniques by replicating the results shown in Figure 9 (Accuracy Dynamics) and Figure 10 (Ablation Study).

Key Findings (Validation of Claims):
1. Figure 9 (Accuracy Dynamics): The reproduction successfully captured the alternating training-verification loop pattern, showing how the model progressively achieves verification by learning from counterexamples.
2. Figure 10 (Ablation Study - Speedup): Despite running in a CPU-only environment (in contrast to the original GPU environment), the core speedup claim was validated. The Ouroboros methodology significantly outperformed the "Vanilla" training-verification loop. For example, the MemManager application showed a 3.0x speedup (47s vs. 143s), confirming the robustness and fundamental efficiency of the spec-aware learning algorithm.

Environment and Modifications:
* Environment: CPU-only (Ubuntu 20.04, Python 3.7+, Julia 1.8.5).
* Critical Modification: A fix was applied to src/tasks.py to handle the device mismatch when loading PyTorch models saved on a GPU: map_location=torch.device('cpu') was added to the load_model function.

This artifact demonstrates the robustness of the Ouroboros system's algorithmic efficiency across different hardware configurations, a key insight for ensuring artifact portability.

long_description: This courselet provides information on using pandas to do data cleaning. Data cleaning is the process of identifying and correcting errors, inconsistencies, and inaccuracies in datasets. It is an important step in the data preparation process before analysis or modeling can be performed. It is a time-consuming process, especially for large datasets. However, the benefits of high-quality data are significant and can improve decision-making, increase efficiency, and reduce costs. Conversely, poor data quality can lead to inaccurate results, incorrect conclusions, and costly mistakes. Data cleaning involves various techniques such as handling missing values, removing duplicates, converting data types, and checking for consistency. These techniques help to ensure that the data is accurate, reliable, and consistent for analysis. This courselet uses a modified version of the [Kaggle Netflix dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/shivamb/netflix-shows) that is available [here](https://github.com/dakoop/fount-data-cleaning/raw/refs/heads/main/netflix-titles.csv.gz).

title: HDFS-17216
short_description: When distcp handle the small files, the bandwidth parameter will be invalid, resulting in serious overspeed behavior
long_description:
When distcp handles small files (file size slightly smaller than bandwidth), the throttler only starts to throttle after 1 second, and the throttled is specific to a single file, causing distcp to fill the cluster bandwidth and crush production traffic. This is a workload scale bug that manifests when processing many small files.

Root Cause: The ThrottledInputStream class has a bug in getBytesPerSec() method where division by zero or very small elapsed time results in incorrect throttling calculations for small files.

title: FLINK-35815
short_description: KinesisProxySyncV2 doesn't always retry throttling exceptions.
long_description:
FLINK-35815, titled "KinesisProxySyncV2 doesn't always retry throttling exceptions," describes a problem where the KinesisProxySyncV2 class fails to retry certain throttling exceptions, specifically LimitExceededException, during DescribeStreamSummary calls to AWS Kinesis. 

The root cause is identified in the AwsV2Util.isRecoverableException method, which only checks the cause of an exception (exception.getCause()) and not the exception itself. As a result, when a LimitExceededException is thrown directly (without being wrapped in another exception), the retry mechanism does not recognize it as recoverable, leading to job failures instead of retries.

The bug report provides a stack trace showing a LimitExceededException causing a FlinkRuntimeException, indicating that the exception was not retried as expected. This issue affects versions like aws-connector-4.2.0, aws-connector-4.3.0, and 1.19.1, with fixes released in aws-connector-4.4.0 and aws-connector-5.0.0.
